opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was a fairly pragmatic decision. In high school I did math competitions and got through the provincial-level selection, but once I was there I could see pretty clearly what the next stage would demand. The people who go further are spending an enormous amount of time grinding on very specialized problem types, things like hard combinatorics and olympiad-style inequalities, and many of them have been training for years. I did a rough self-assessment and felt that even if I put in a huge effort, the odds of going much further weren't great, and the opportunity cost was very high.

At the same time, I'd started getting into computers and programming, and that felt much more exciting to me. With math competitions you solve a problem and that's it. With programming you can build something, run it, and see it actually do things. That feedback loop really hooked me. So instead of forcing myself to keep climbing in math, I shifted my energy toward informatics and computer science more broadly.

Looking back, I don't regret it at all. The math training gave me a solid foundation, the habit of thinking rigorously and staying patient with hard problems, and that's been really useful in machine learning and reinforcement learning. But I think knowing when to stop and redirect your effort toward something you're more passionate about, and where you have a comparative advantage, is an important skill. That was probably one of my first real experiences making that kind of trade-off.

r001.rationale: The response cites the time demands, low perceived odds, opportunity cost, and interest in programming. It does not attribute the decision to a lack of competition-training foundation at his school.

r002.rationale: The response says others had trained for years and describes specialized problem types, but does not say his difficulty came from not encountering those problems early enough.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it was a pretty practical decision. I did math competitions through middle school and into high school, and I made it to the provincial selection stage, but once I got there I could see pretty clearly where I stood. The people who go on to the national team level are operating at a different speed. They see the trick in a problem in thirty seconds, and I'd still be setting it up. I could grind and improve, but I wasn't going to close that gap with effort alone.

At the same time, I had started messing around with programming, and that felt completely different. In math competitions, there's a fixed answer and someone decides whether you got it. In programming, you write something, you run it, and it either works or it doesn't. The feedback loop is immediate, and you can build things that actually do something. That was a lot more satisfying to me than spending another two years on olympiad geometry.

So I kind of redirected that energy. Competition math gave me a good foundation for thinking rigorously, and that carried over into informatics competitions and later into research. But I didn't see the point in pushing further in a direction where I knew my ceiling. It was better to find something where I could keep going up.

r001.rationale: The candidate cites a perceived gap in problem-solving speed and greater satisfaction with programming, but does not mention a lack of competition-training foundation at his school.

r002.rationale: The candidate says he was slower to spot tricks and doubted effort would close the gap, but does not attribute this difficulty to encountering advanced problems too late.

astra-6.text: I enjoyed math, but enjoying math and wanting to commit to competitions were different things for me. At that stage, I felt I would need to put much more time into preparation to keep going, and I wasn’t sure that was how I wanted to spend the rest of high school. I wanted room to explore other interests, so I decided not to pursue the next stage.

r001.rationale: The response cites the time commitment and desire to explore other interests, but does not mention a lack of competition-training foundation at his school.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention difficulty with problems above the provincial-selection level or having encountered them too late.
